a-weak-acid-breaks-the-naive-sum: A litre of water, so the arithmetic stays a clean 0.1 mol/L.
0.1 mol of acetic acid dissolves — the same count of acid molecules a strong acid would bring.
The meter reads about 2.9: most of that acetic acid is still whole, still holding its proton.
A second beaker, for the comparison that makes the point.
The same litre of water, so only the acid differs.
The same 0.1 mol, this time of hydrochloric acid.
This meter reads about 1.1. Same count, same water, nearly two pH units apart — the difference is how much of each acid lets go.
catalyst-area-and-stirring-change-the-ra: 100 mL of water in the first flask.
0.1 mol of peroxide — the amount every flask will get, so only the catalyst and the stirring can differ.
A pinch of manganese dioxide: 0.1 g, the reference loading.
A second flask joins the bench, for ten times as much catalyst.
Ten times the catalyst — 1 g — which is ten times the surface the peroxide can meet.
A third flask, for the reference pinch stirred much faster.
The reference 0.1 g of catalyst again, so here only the stirring will change.
The first flask stirs for one second at 500 rpm: this is the rate the other two are measured against.
The second stirs identically and decomposes more in the same second — more exposed area, more reaction.
The third stirs ten times faster on the reference pinch. It does gain, but far less than tenfold: the help from stirring levels off.
cold-pack: 100 mL of water, and the thermometer starts at room temperature.
The potassium chloride dissolves and the thermometer falls a few degrees. Dissolving can take heat in as readily as it gives it out.
crystallising-salt-from-brine: A litre of water goes into the beaker.
117 g of salt — two moles — dissolves completely, well under what a litre can hold.
Four fifths of the water boils away. The 200 mL left cannot hold two moles, so solid salt appears at the bottom.
Look at what is there: white crystals under a solution that is now saturated, not a dry beaker.
filtering-a-precipitate: 100 mL of water to work in.
The sodium chloride dissolves and the beaker stays clear.
Silver nitrate meets the chloride and the beaker goes cloudy — that solid is silver chloride, and it is no longer dissolved.
A second vessel is set out to catch whatever runs through.
Pour it through the paper: the solid stays behind, the liquid runs into v2.
Look at v1: the silver chloride is held on the paper, which is how a precipitate gets weighed.
Look at v2: clear, but not pure water — the sodium and nitrate ions ran straight through with it.
hot-pack: 100 mL of water, and the thermometer starts at room temperature.
The calcium chloride dissolves and the thermometer climbs about 20 °C. Nothing burned — dissolving itself released the heat.
ph-is-not-quite-minus-log-c: A litre of water, so the arithmetic stays a clean 0.1 mol/L.
0.1 mol of hydrochloric acid dissolves completely, giving 0.100 mol/L of hydrogen ions by count.
The meter reads about 1.08, not the 1.00 the formula predicts. The reading repeats, so the gap is the activity correction and not an error.
sugar-syrup-by-density: 100 mL of water goes into the beaker; on its own it weighs 99.70 g.
25 g of sugar dissolves and disappears from sight — but it has not left the beaker.
The balance reads 124.70 g, the sum of both. The sugar is still in there, and the syrup is now denser than the water it started as.
the-antacid-runs-on-arithmetic: 100 mL of water to make the mock stomach acid in.
0.01 mol of hydrochloric acid: the beaker is now sharply acidic, around pH 1.
One gram of bicarbonate is 0.0119 mol — more than the acid. It fizzes off carbon dioxide, the acid runs out first, and the pH settles near 9.
the-series-decides-who-plates: 100 mL of water for the copper salt to dissolve in.
Copper sulfate dissolves and the solution turns blue: the colour belongs to the copper ions in it.
Zinc goes in and trades places with the copper. Copper plates onto the strip, the blue drains out of the solution, and the beaker heats to about 60 °C.
three-beakers-of-peroxide: The first flask gets 100 mL of water — the control, which will be given nothing else.
0.1 mol of hydrogen peroxide dissolves in it. It is already unstable, but nothing here hurries it.
A second flask joins the bench, so the comparison runs side by side rather than one after the other.
The same 100 mL of water: only one thing may differ between the flasks.
The same 0.1 mol of peroxide, so any difference later belongs to what comes next.
Half a gram of manganese dioxide goes in — a catalyst, which lowers the barrier without being used up.
A third flask, for the catalyst living things use.
And the same peroxide, for the third time.
A thousandth of a gram of catalase is all the third flask gets — a hundred-thousandth of the peroxide's mass.
One second passes for all three. The plain flask has done nothing the bench will report, the manganese flask has decomposed a little, and the catalase flask has already finished.
vinegar-and-baking-soda: 250 mL of water goes into the beaker — the solvent the powder and the acid will meet in.
The bicarbonate dissolves and simply waits: nothing bubbles yet, because there is no acid here to hand it a proton.
Now the acetic acid arrives and the bubbles start — that is carbon dioxide leaving the open beaker, which is why the vessel gets lighter.
